title: B200 smoke results (Feb 2026) — early bring-up + limited benchmark matrix
linked_artifacts: GitHub(redwood): pr-24927 (B200 SKU detection + compatibility gate)
content:
Context / intent
- This is an early B200 bring-up smoke pass to validate basic correctness + rough performance order-of-magnitude.
- Not a full acceptance matrix (noise high; some runs on mismatched driver/CUDA; kernel fallbacks currently common).
- Goal: identify blockers for profile pack defaults + compatibility gates before expanding fleet.

Test window
- 2026-02-06 to 2026-02-19
- Most stable data points are from 2026-02-18/19 after driver alignment on 2 nodes.

Environment
- Hardware: early-access NVIDIA B200 nodes (SXM form factor), 8x GPU, ~192GB HBM per GPU (reported 196,608 MiB)
- Interconnect: NVLink present (not heavily exercised in these single-GPU smoke runs)
- Runtime branch: runtime-1.22 RC candidates
- Profile pack: b200 preview profiles (requires explicit pin; runtime refuses unsafe implicit defaults)
- Notes: numbers below are per-GPU and single-replica unless stated

Software versions observed (this was a major source of variance)
- Node cohort A (problematic): Driver 560.35.xx, CUDA runtime in container 12.4
  - Symptoms: “no kernel image available for execution on the device” for some fused kernels; high fallback rates; occasional init failures.
- Node cohort B (better): Driver 570.42.xx, CUDA runtime in container 12.5
  - Symptoms: stable launch; still elevated attention kernel fallbacks (expected until sm_100 tuned kernels are fully wired)

Compatibility gate status (as of pr-24927)
- Gate behavior: if GPU SKU=B200 and profile_version not explicitly pinned, runtime will refuse to start.
- Gate behavior: if driver < 570.* OR container CUDA < 12.5, runtime starts only in “safe mode” (forces conservative kernels + smaller batching caps) and emits a loud warning + metric flag.
- Action item: enforce these gates in Private installer as well (tracked separately).

What we ran (limited smoke matrix)
Workloads are intentionally small. We tested a few prompt/response buckets at low concurrency.

Workload buckets
- S1 (short): prompt 128, output 128
- M1 (medium): prompt 1024, output 256
- L1 (long prefill): prompt 8192, output 128

Models
- llama-3.1-8b-instruct (fp16)
- qwen2.5-14b-instruct (fp16)
- llama-3.1-70b-instruct (int8 weights, fp16 activations; single GPU feasibility depends on KV settings; some runs were disabled)

Key metrics captured
- Request latency: p50 / p95 / p99 (ms)
- Throughput: decode tok/s (steady-state) and prefill tok/s (approx; see notes)
- GPU util (%, average over run)
- Peak HBM (GiB)
- Kernel fallback rate (% of attention ops not using preferred kernel)
- Scheduler queue time (ms) where available

IMPORTANT measurement caveats
- For B200 we saw higher variance run-to-run than H100/L40S (likely due to kernel selection churn + driver mismatches early).
- Prefill tok/s is derived from stage timing + token counts; treat as directional only in this document.
- “Kernel fallback rate” is from kernel_choice counters; early instrumentation does not distinguish “expected fallback” vs “unexpected fallback” well.

3) llama-3.1-70b-instruct (int8 weights, fp16 activations)
- Status: INCONCLUSIVE in this smoke pass.
- On cohort A, we saw repeated kernel launch failures during warmup.
- On cohort B, we were able to load with conservative KV settings, but throughput/latency varied strongly with allocator compaction settings.
- Recommendation: do not publish any 70B B200 “expected behavior” numbers based on this sheet.

| 2026-02-18 | B      | 1    | S1     | 410    | 520    | 620    | 62k           | 1,750        | 61         | 86.4         | 33%                    | load ok; decode ok; fallback elevated |

Bring-up issues observed
1) Driver/CUDA mismatches (highest impact)
- Symptom A: runtime init failure or “no kernel image available” for certain fused ops.
- Symptom B: attention kernels silently falling back to generic implementation (large perf drop; tail latency increases under concurrency).
- Observed correlation: cohort A fallback rates 35–45% vs cohort B 14–31%.
- Needed actions:
  - Infra: standardize B200 nodes on >= 570.* driver line and document exceptions.
  - Release: ensure runtime container images used for B200 are built with CUDA 12.5 toolchain and include sm_100 fatbins.
  - Runtime: keep compatibility gate strict (fail closed) for Hosted defaults until baseline is consistent.

2) Kernel fallback rates higher than we want (even on “good” cohort)
- Current behavior: preferred attention kernel not always selected; long-context bucket (L1) triggers more fallback.
- Hypotheses (needs validation):
  - missing sm_100 specialization for attention v3 path; using H100-tuned heuristics
  - conservative guardrails in selection logic treat unknown sm_100 edge cases as unsafe and force generic
  - some sequence length ranges not covered by tuned kernel dispatch table
- Immediate follow-ups:
  - Add breakdown metrics: fallback_by_reason (capability, seq_len, head_dim, kv_layout, other).
  - Add a “kernel choice summary” line to startup log (Yuki already prototyping similar for H100).

3) Instability with certain fused ops on cohort A
- We saw a crash on qwen2.5-14b warmup in one run when fused RMSNorm was enabled.
- This did not reproduce on cohort B.
- Treat as “driver/toolchain mismatch” until proven otherwise.

4) Scheduler queue time instrumentation gaps
- On some runs scheduler_queue_ms was missing (older runtime build).
- Without queue time, it’s hard to separate true compute regressions vs queue/backpressure.
- Action: require scheduler_queue_ms for any future B200 perf runs (even smoke).

5) Memory headroom + fragmentation sensitivity for long-context
- For L1, peak HBM climbed rapidly as conc increased beyond 2–4 even for 8B/14B.
- Long-context runs had higher p99 jitter; compaction counters suggested allocator churn.
- This is likely expected until KV cache/allocator defaults are tuned for B200.

Interpretation (very rough)
- When driver/CUDA are aligned (cohort B), B200 looks promising on small models (8B/14B):
  - p50 improved materially vs cohort A
  - decode tok/s improved ~35–45% vs cohort A on these tests
- But “good cohort” still shows non-trivial attention kernel fallback rates and long-context sensitivity.
- Biggest risk for rollout is not average throughput; it’s tail behavior under mixed workloads + kernel dispatch churn.

Recommended next steps (to unblock profile pack + expected behavior docs)
1) Infra (owner: Irene Choi)
- Lock B200 baseline:
  - driver >= 570.*
  - container CUDA toolchain 12.5
- Provide a list of any unavoidable exceptions and how runtime should surface them (label + metric).

2) Runtime kernel selection (owner: Hiro Tanaka / Yuki Sato)
- Add per-reason fallback metrics.
- Expand tuned kernel dispatch table for sm_100 and long-context shapes.
- Define an explicit “acceptable fallback rate” for smoke vs full benchmark.

3) Benchmark-lab (owner: Rina Kobayashi)
- Expand matrix slightly once baseline is stable:
  - add conc=16 for S1 on 8B/14B
  - add one mid-context bucket (prompt 4096, output 256)
  - repeat runs across 2 regions to measure variance
- Keep B200 suite allowed-to-fail until fallback rate is under control.

4) Profiles / gates (owner: Quentin Harris)
- Maintain hard requirement for explicit profile pin for B200.
- Add “b200_safe_mode” bit to the profile selection summary, and ensure it’s visible in /health debug output.

Appendix: run metadata (for reproducibility)
- benchmark-lab job names (subset):
  - b200_smoke_llama31_8b_s1_c1_2026-02-19
  - b200_smoke_llama31_8b_s1_c8_2026-02-19
  - b200_smoke_qwen25_14b_m1_c4_2026-02-19
- runtime build identifiers:
  - cohort A: runtime-1.22-rc0 (git sha unknown; local build on 2026-02-08)
  - cohort B: runtime-1.22-rc2 (built 2026-02-18; includes pr-24927)

Open questions
- What is the minimal acceptable driver/CUDA spread we can tolerate for Dedicated B200 (if customers bring their own nodes in Private)?
- Do we want to expose “safe mode” vs “full mode” to customers, or keep it internal and just document supported baselines?
- For long context, should the default B200 profile prioritize headroom (lower concurrency caps) until kernel fallbacks are addressed?
